title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 4
description: 57-year-old female client with a first seizure in adulthood from a left frontotemporal glioblastoma: signs of increased ICP, glioblastoma vs meningioma vs brain metastasis, focal impaired awareness to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, vasogenic vs cytotoxic edema, Monro-Kellie components and hydrocephalus types, status epilepticus after craniotomy, and corticosteroid complications at discharge.

authorReview.note:
New case written by Claude on 2 Nov 2026 for the Unit 7 learning outcomes; please review before using it with students:
- Learning outcomes: brain tumour types, seizure classification, vasogenic vs cytotoxic edema, Monro-Kellie components and causes of increased ICP, non-communicating vs communicating hydrocephalus.
- Screen 4 is a knowledge matrix framed as care planning (which volume each factor increases); please confirm it fits your Generate Solutions expectations.
- The capillary glucose target (4.0–7.0 mmol/L before meals) is the Diabetes Canada target, not an MCC laboratory range.
- Clinician review: dexamethasone, levetiracetam and lorazepam doses.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes

highlightTabs.content: 1910:{T 37.0° C}, {P 92 beats/min}, {RR 18 breaths/min}, {BP 142/86 mm Hg}, {SpO₂ 97% on room air}.

question.explanation:
Suggest increased ICP:

Headache worst on waking and with coughing or bending: lying flat overnight and mild CO₂ retention during sleep increase cerebral blood volume; coughing and bending raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous drainage from the head.

Vomiting on waking without nausea (often projectile): pressure on the vomiting centre in the medulla.

Bilateral papilledema: swelling of the optic discs because raised CSF pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths; a reliable sign of sustained raised ICP.

Not signs of increased ICP: staring, lip smacking, tongue biting and urinary incontinence are features of the seizure; the glucose rules out hypoglycemia as the cause of the seizure. The vital signs are not those of Cushing's triad (a late sign). Her drowsiness may be postictal or due to ICP, and the personality change, word-finding difficulty and right-hand weakness are focal deficits from the lesion itself; the nurse trends all of them.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Diagnostic Results.
question.stem: The client's husband asks what kind of tumor this might be. For each feature, click to specify whether it is typical of a glioblastoma, a meningioma, or a brain metastasis. Each feature may apply to more than one tumor.

rows.text: Arises from the meninges (arachnoid cells), outside the brain tissue
Arises from glial cells (astrocytes) within the brain tissue
Spreads to the brain through the blood from cancers such as lung, breast, or melanoma
Can cause seizures, headache, and focal neurological deficits
Usually benign and slow-growing; often cured by complete removal
Ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding edema on MRI
Infiltrates the surrounding brain, so complete removal is rarely possible
Most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults

question.explanation:
Gliomas arise from the glial (supporting) cells of the brain: astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas and ependymomas. Glioblastoma (grade 4 astrocytoma) is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in adults. It grows quickly, has a necrotic centre with ring enhancement, and sends cells along white matter tracts, so it cannot be removed completely and usually recurs; treatment is surgery, then radiation with temozolomide chemotherapy.

Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cells of the meninges and press on the brain from outside (extra-axial, dural-based). They are the most common primary intracranial tumor, are usually benign and slow-growing, and are often cured by complete removal, but their location can still cause seizures, headache and deficits. Other tumor types include pituitary adenomas and vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas).

Brain metastases are the most common brain tumors overall in adults. Cancer cells reach the brain through the blood (most often from lung, breast, melanoma, kidney and colon) and are often multiple, at the grey-white matter junction, with ring enhancement and edema; that is why her chest, abdomen and pelvis were scanned.

Any brain tumor can raise ICP (mass and edema), irritate the cortex (seizures) and cause deficits according to its location.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The seizure the husband described is best classified as a [[drop0]]. The client's signs of increased ICP are mainly caused by [[drop1]], which results from [[drop2]] and is expected to improve with [[drop3]].

options.text: focal impaired awareness seizure that progressed to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
failure of the sodium-potassium pump in oxygen-deprived brain cells
abnormal tumor blood vessels that let plasma leak through a damaged blood-brain barrier
blocked CSF absorption at the arachnoid villi

question.explanation:
Seizure type: the seizure began in one hemisphere (the left temporal lobe near the tumor): staring and unresponsiveness (impaired awareness) with automatisms (lip smacking, picking at clothing with the right hand) is a focal impaired awareness seizure (formerly complex partial). It then spread to both hemispheres: a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (formerly secondarily generalized). A generalized-onset seizure involves both hemispheres from the start, without a focal beginning; an absence seizure is a brief stare without convulsions; in a focal aware seizure the person stays aware. A new seizure starting in adulthood always needs a search for a structural cause such as a tumor.

Vasogenic edema: the tumor makes new, abnormal blood vessels whose walls lack normal tight junctions, so the blood-brain barrier leaks plasma proteins and water into the extracellular space, mostly in the white matter around the tumor. Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) stabilize the barrier and reduce this edema within hours to days.

Cytotoxic edema is different: oxygen-deprived cells (ischemia, hypoxia, prolonged seizures) cannot run the sodium-potassium pump, so sodium and water enter the cells and they swell, in grey and white matter; it does not respond to corticosteroids. Levetiracetam prevents seizures but does not reduce edema; hypotonic fluids worsen edema.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Provider Orders.
question.stem: The nurse plans care to keep the client's ICP from rising further. For each factor, click to specify which intracranial volume it increases: brain tissue, blood, or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

rows.text: Vasogenic edema around the tumor
Hypoventilation from oversedation, raising the PaCO₂
A tumor blocking the cerebral aqueduct (non-communicating hydrocephalus)
Neck flexion or rotation that compresses the jugular veins
Cytotoxic edema after a prolonged seizure with hypoxia
Scarring of the arachnoid villi that impairs CSF absorption (communicating hydrocephalus)
Fever, which increases brain metabolism

question.explanation:
Monro-Kellie doctrine: the skull holds brain tissue (about 80%), blood (about 10%) and CSF (about 10%). An increase in any one must be offset by a decrease in another, or ICP rises. The nurse plans care around all three.

Brain tissue: the tumor mass and edema. Vasogenic edema is treated with dexamethasone; cytotoxic edema after a long seizure with hypoxia is prevented by stopping seizures quickly and keeping oxygenation normal (seizure precautions, levetiracetam on time).

Blood: CO₂ is a strong cerebral vasodilator, so hypoventilation (oversedation, opioids) raises cerebral blood volume; sedation is monitored. A flexed or rotated neck obstructs jugular venous outflow; the head is kept midline with the head of the bed at 30 degrees. Fever and seizures increase metabolism and therefore cerebral blood flow; fever is treated promptly.

CSF: CSF builds up if its flow is blocked inside the ventricular system (non-communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus, for example a tumor at the cerebral aqueduct or fourth ventricle) or if it is not absorbed by the arachnoid villi (communicating hydrocephalus, after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage). Her ventricles are not enlarged now, but headache, vomiting and drowsiness after surgery could signal hydrocephalus and are reported.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 3 1500 and Day 4 0710 and the Provider Orders from Day 3 1500.
question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Call for help and notify the provider
Apply oxygen and have suction ready
Withhold medication until the seizure has lasted 15 minutes
Insert a padded tongue blade between her teeth
Turn the client onto her side
Restrain her arms and legs to prevent injury

question.explanation:
The seizure has lasted more than 5 minutes: this is status epilepticus, a medical emergency. The longer it lasts, the less likely it is to stop on its own, and continuous neuronal firing causes hypoxia, excitotoxic (cytotoxic) brain injury and rising ICP.

Correct: a side-lying position lets saliva drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway. Lorazepam is the first-line drug and is given at 5 minutes, as ordered. Oxygen and suction treat the hypoxia (dusky lips). Hypoglycemia can cause or prolong seizures, and dexamethasone affects glucose, so the glucose is checked. Help is needed to manage the airway, drugs and monitoring, and the provider must be notified.

Incorrect: restraints can cause fractures and soft tissue injury; nearby objects are moved and the head is protected instead. Nothing is put in the mouth. Waiting to treat lets the seizure become harder to stop and the brain injury worse.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it shows that an expected outcome has been met or that it requires follow-up.

rows.text: No seizures since Day 4
Capillary glucose 14.8 mmol/L before supper
Headache 2/10 with no vomiting
“I'll stop the dexamethasone once my headaches are gone.”
White patches on the tongue and inner cheeks
“I won't drive until my doctor tells me it's safe.”
Husband's plan for managing a seizure at home
Incision clean and dry, staples intact

question.explanation:
Outcomes met: no further seizures on the increased levetiracetam dose; less headache and no vomiting (edema and ICP reduced after resection and dexamethasone); a healing incision. In Canada, a seizure leads to a period without driving set by provincial rules and the provider, and she understands this. The husband's plan is correct: protect, side-lying, time the seizure, and call 911 at 5 minutes.

Require follow-up: dexamethasone-induced hyperglycemia (glucocorticoids raise hepatic glucose production and insulin resistance) needs to be reported for treatment. White patches that do not wipe off suggest oral candidiasis (thrush) from corticosteroid immunosuppression. Stopping dexamethasone suddenly can cause adrenal insufficiency and rebound cerebral edema: it must be tapered as prescribed, so this statement needs further teaching.
